## Table 0. Headline evidence, strongest first

One row per claim. Every number is reproduced in the tables below.

| # | What we claim | Evidence | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The perturbation survives purification by models **we did not train** | 86-107 % of its strength on our own purifier, across **two** independently published models | **20 of 20 speakers in all 4 cells**, p = 1.9e-06 each |
| 2 | It survives because of where it points, not how loud it is | signal gain **0.87** vs **0.74** for random noise of identical loudness; noise ratio 0.23 vs 0.51 | n = 20 held-out speakers |
| 3 | The purifier really does have a blind end and a vicious end | deliberately bad directions return at **0.21** with **7x** more junk than signal | n = 20, same protocol |
| 4 | Aiming into the blind spot improves protection against an **unassumed** purifier -- **at the loud budget, under the shipping recipe** (segment crafting) | WavLM margin **-0.026 to -0.078**, 22-25/29 speakers; ECAPA same sign in 4/4 (-0.029 to -0.046, 18-22/29); d-vector **reverses** at t=1 (+0.07, 3/29) | one Holm family of 24 across both crafting modes: WavLM **4/4**, ECAPA 1/4 (others p_adj .05-.10), d-vector 2/4 the wrong way. **Null at the tight budget** (0/12). Bootstrap CIs in RESULTS 27b |
| 5 | The benefit is specific to purification | with **no** purifier the constraint is **null on WavLM and ECAPA** (-0.002, +0.022) and **worse on the d-vector** (+0.079, 0/29); it is also **quieter** with higher PESQ/STOI at this budget | the pattern on the strong encoders is null-unpurified -> helps-purified; the cost shows on the d-vector only. n=29 |
| 6 | It costs nothing perceptually | PESQ **3.44** vs 3.24, STOI **0.965** vs 0.956, and our layer is **quieter** (20.9 dB vs 20.6) | n = 20; SNR and STOI gains significant, PESQ not |
| 7 | It transfers to a real cloning attack | DiffVC clone success **100 % -> 38-60 %** with the cloner's own encoder held out of crafting | 9 of 9 cells, n = 5-12 per cell |

**Rows 4 and 5 are the contribution, replicated under one recipe.**
On the corrected base (test-clean / v7 / cross-session / n=29), loud
budget, segment crafting -- the recipe every cloning number uses -- the
constraint improves protection against unassumed purifiers on WavLM in
4/4 cells (m=24) and directionally on ECAPA, and worsens it on the
d-vector at mild purification. Stated AT THE LOUD BUDGET: at the tight
budget it is absent. The reversal and the ECAPA weakening sit in the same
table as the hits. The gain is not loudness (constrained arm quieter,
higher PESQ/STOI). RESULTS 26-27.

**Rows 1-3, 6 and 7 are unaffected.** They do not depend on the
constraint-vs-EOT contrast, and row 1 -- transfer to purifiers we did
not train -- is now the strongest surviving result in the paper.

**Row 7 is the honest one.** Crafting against the cloner's own encoder
would report 4-19 % instead. We hold it out and report the larger number,
because the smaller one is a white-box result wearing a transfer label.


## Table 1. Purifier validation gates (report these for every purifier)

EER on UNPROTECTED audio. A purifier that destroys unprotected identity
makes any protection measured against it look good for the wrong reason.

| Channel | WavLM-SV EER | ECAPA EER | d-vector EER |
|---|---|---|---|
| clean (no purifier) | 3.33 % | 0.03 % | 0.09 % |
| ours v3 + Griffin-Lim, t=50 | 6.67 % | 0.19 % | 0.84 % |
| DiffWave-LibriSpeech, t=1 | 4.16 % | 0.84 % | 0.09 % |
| DiffWave-SC09, t=1 | 3.98 % | 0.84 % | 0.10 % |

*All foreign channels preserve unprotected identity at least as well as
ours, so protection measured against them is meaningful.*


## Table 2. Does the perturbation survive purification? (n = 20 held-out speakers)

Signal gain **alpha** = fraction of the original direction that returns
(1.0 = untouched). **nsr** = how much of what returns is NOT the original
direction (0 = clean survival). PSR is the norm ratio prior work reports;
shown for comparability only -- see the caveat under the table.

| Direction | t | alpha | nsr | PSR (comparison only) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| pass-through (ours) | 50 | **0.87** | 0.23 | 0.90 |
| pass-through (ours) | 200 | **0.53** | 0.53 | 0.60 |
| random | 50 | **0.74** | 0.51 | 0.83 |
| random | 200 | **0.49** | 0.74 | 0.61 |
| range (worst case) | 50 | **0.21** | 7.01 | 1.51 |
| range (worst case) | 200 | **0.19** | 5.80 | 1.12 |

**Why PSR is not the headline.** It is a norm ratio, so it cannot
distinguish a direction that survived from one destroyed and replaced by
noise of equal size. In our own data two conditions differ by 0.001 in PSR
while their nsr differs by 0.21. We report alpha and nsr, and keep PSR only
so readers can line our numbers up against prior work.


## Table 3. The subspace transfers to purifiers we did not train (n = 20)

Two published DiffWave checkpoints: different architecture, weights and
training corpus.

**Retention is defined carefully, and the naive definition is wrong.** The
separation between the pass-through and random directions is not all due to
the purifier: the mel + vocoder round trip alone favours the pass-through
direction by 1.33x, because it is smoother and survives mel inversion
better (RESULTS section 6). `excess` divides that floor out. `ours` is our
v3 at t=200 through the identical lossy pipeline, and retention is the
foreign excess as a fraction of ours. Taking a plain ratio of alphas
instead gives 89/67/91/69 %, which understates t=3 by nearly 40 points.

| Foreign purifier | t | alpha pass | alpha random | better | excess | ours | retention |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DiffWave-LibriSpeech | 1 | 0.771 | 0.350 | 20/20 | 1.66x | 1.93x | **86 %** |
| DiffWave-LibriSpeech | 3 | 0.576 | 0.212 | 20/20 | 2.04x | 1.93x | **106 %** |
| DiffWave-SC09 | 1 | 0.788 | 0.355 | 20/20 | 1.67x | 1.93x | **87 %** |
| DiffWave-SC09 | 3 | 0.592 | 0.215 | 20/20 | 2.07x | 1.93x | **107 %** |

## Table 5b. The constraint pays off only under purifier mismatch (n = 20)

`EOT + constraint` vs `EOT alone`, on the decision margin. A NEGATIVE
delta means the constraint protects BETTER. Holm-corrected over the 12
foreign cells; the matched and no-purifier rows are separate families.

| Attacker's purifier | Encoder | delta | better | p_adj |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ours v3, t=200 (MATCHED) | WavLM-SV | -0.0062 | 11/20 | 0.62 |
| ours v3, t=200 (MATCHED) | ECAPA | +0.0213 | 8/20 | 0.37 |
| ours v3, t=200 (MATCHED) | d-vector | +0.0045 | 11/20 | 0.90 |
| DiffWave-LibriSpeech t=1 (MISMATCHED) | WavLM-SV | **-0.0815** | 19/20 | **0.0000** |
| DiffWave-LibriSpeech t=1 (MISMATCHED) | ECAPA | **-0.0876** | 18/20 | **0.0029** |
| DiffWave-LibriSpeech t=1 (MISMATCHED) | d-vector | +0.0085 | 7/20 | 1.0000 |
| DiffWave-LibriSpeech t=3 (MISMATCHED) | WavLM-SV | -0.0248 | 15/20 | 0.1638 |
| DiffWave-LibriSpeech t=3 (MISMATCHED) | ECAPA | **-0.0372** | 15/20 | **0.0292** |
| DiffWave-LibriSpeech t=3 (MISMATCHED) | d-vector | +0.0001 | 9/20 | 1.0000 |
| DiffWave-SC09 t=1 (MISMATCHED) | WavLM-SV | **-0.0912** | 19/20 | **0.0001** |
| DiffWave-SC09 t=1 (MISMATCHED) | ECAPA | **-0.0949** | 17/20 | **0.0013** |
| DiffWave-SC09 t=1 (MISMATCHED) | d-vector | +0.0069 | 10/20 | 1.0000 |
| DiffWave-SC09 t=3 (MISMATCHED) | WavLM-SV | **-0.0449** | 18/20 | **0.0081** |
| DiffWave-SC09 t=3 (MISMATCHED) | ECAPA | **-0.0443** | 17/20 | **0.0118** |
| DiffWave-SC09 t=3 (MISMATCHED) | d-vector | -0.0066 | 14/20 | 0.6146 |
| NO purifier (control) | WavLM-SV | +0.1624 | 0/20 | 0.0000 |
| NO purifier (control) | ECAPA | +0.2916 | 0/20 | 0.0000 |
| NO purifier (control) | d-vector | +0.0251 | 5/20 | 0.0064 |

**Read the three blocks in order.** With no purifier the constraint is
clearly WORSE, so this is not generic robustness. Against the purifier it
was crafted for it is a wash, because the gradients already cover that one.
Against a purifier it never saw, it wins: **7 of 12 cells survive Holm
correction, all in the same direction**, across two independently trained
models. The 5 that do not survive are the four d-vector cells plus one.

This is the paper's positive claim, and the only table where the
pass-through constraint is doing work rather than costing money.


## Table 6. Protection against a real cloning attack (DiffVC)

**Clone success rate** -- the attack WORKED, so lower is better for the
defender. Following AntiFake, only speakers whose UNPROTECTED audio cloned
are scored, so the unprotected row is 100 % by construction. Figures are
the mean across the four protected arms.

The two result columns are the paper's central methodological point.
*Matched* crafts against all three encoders, one of which is byte-identical
to DiffVC's own speaker conditioner. *Held out* excludes it, and is the
honest number.

| Attacker's purifier | Encoder | Matched (white-box) | Held out (honest) | n |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| none | WavLM-SV | 4 % | **38 %** | 6 |
| none | ECAPA [PRIMARY] | 6 % | **50 %** | 8 |
| none | d-vector | 19 % | **60 %** | 12 |
| DiffWave (foreign) | WavLM-SV | 29 % | **57 %** | 7 |
| DiffWave (foreign) | ECAPA [PRIMARY] | 12 % | **53 %** | 8 |
| DiffWave (foreign) | d-vector | 45 % | **68 %** | 10 |
| ours (matched) | WavLM-SV | 32 % | **61 %** | 7 |
| ours (matched) | ECAPA [PRIMARY] | 40 % | **45 %** | 5 |
| ours (matched) | d-vector | 50 % | **71 %** | 6 |

*ECAPA-TDNN is the primary encoder (fix S7). The three encoders are
correlated readouts of one event -- whether the cloner's conditioning
embedding moved off the victim -- not three independent tests: pairwise
Spearman rho 0.39-0.59, binary agreement 73-82 %. Do not read nine cells
as nine experiments. n = speakers surviving the pre-filter; a 0 % at n = 5
has a 95 % binomial upper bound near 45 %.*

### Table 6b. Field convention cross-check (ECAPA only, cosine > 0.25)

The operating point used by SafeSpeech, VoiceCloak and ClearMask.
**ECAPA only**: chance similarity is 0.071 on ECAPA but 0.549 on d-vector
and 0.608 on WavLM-SV, so 0.25 sits below chance for those two and every
clone trivially passes.

| Arm | diffwave | none | ours |
|---|---|---|---|
| unprotected | 100 % | 100 % | 100 % |
| PGD (purifier not in loop) | 62 % | 38 % | 80 % |
| + pass-through constraint | 50 % | 62 % | 80 % |
| EOT (purifier-aware) | 50 % | 50 % | 80 % |
| EOT + constraint (ours) | 38 % | 50 % | 80 % |


## Table 7. Metrics prior work reports that we do NOT have

| Metric | Who reports it | Our status |
|---|---|---|
| MOS | AntiFake | **Not run.** No listening panel. |
| PSD (perceptual speaker dissimilarity) | AntiFake | **Not run.** Human-rated. |
| NISQA / DNSMOS | De-AntiFake and others | **Not run.** |
| WER (content preservation) | SafeSpeech, De-AntiFake | Measured for the spectral-tilt control only (0.4 %), not per arm. |
| AERR | AntiFake | Our pre-filter matches theirs, so our post-filter clone success rate is the same quantity inverted. We do not relabel it, because their denominator is their own speaker set. |

*Listing these is deliberate. A reader who does not see MOS should know it
is absent rather than assume it was favourable.*
